text: Model United Nations (MUN) is a role-play of the real United Nations. You speak for a country, and you work with the other delegates in your committee on a real world problem until the committee votes on a plan to solve it.

stepsIntro: Every committee follows these steps, in this order. Your chairs run each one and tell you what comes next, so you don't need to remember it all.

steps.title: Roll call
steps.text: The chair reads out every country in the committee. When you hear yours, raise your placard and say "present", or "present and voting" if you promise not to abstain in the final vote.

steps.title: Setting the agenda
steps.text: If the committee has more than one topic, it votes on which one to discuss first. With one topic, this step takes a minute.

steps.title: General Speakers List
steps.text: Delegates add their country to a list and take turns giving a short speech on what their country thinks. Your opening speech goes here.

steps.title: Moderated caucus
steps.text: A shorter debate on one part of the topic. A delegate suggests it, the committee votes, and then the chair picks speakers one at a time.

steps.title: Unmoderated caucus
steps.text: Free time to leave your seat and talk. Find the countries that agree with you and start writing your ideas down together.

steps.title: Working papers
steps.text: Each group of countries writes its ideas on paper. A working paper is a first draft, so it doesn't need a set format.

steps.title: Draft resolution
steps.text: When a working paper is rewritten in the proper format, with countries signed up to support it, it becomes a draft resolution. The committee debates it and can change it.

steps.title: Voting by placard
steps.text: The chair asks who is for, who is against and who abstains, and you raise your placard each time. If more countries vote for it than against, the draft resolution passes.

checklistIntro: Do these in the weeks before {date}.

checklist.title: Read your background guide.
checklist.text: It explains your committee's topic. Find it on your committee's page or on Resources once it's released.

checklist.title: Research your country's view.
checklist.text: What has your country said or done about the topic? The research links on Resources are a good place to start.

checklist.title: Write a 60 to 90-second opening speech.
checklist.text: Say who you are, what your country thinks and what you'd like the committee to do. Practise it out loud with a timer.

checklist.title: Come to the lead-in.
checklist.text: The day before the conference, 29 October, your committee meets its Executive Board for a short session to get ready. Time and place TBC.

onTheDay.title: What to bring
items: Your opening speech and research notes
Your laptop, if you'd like to use one in committee

onTheDay.title: Your phone
items: You can bring your phone, but you can only use it at set times during committee sessions.
The exact phone rule is TBC.

onTheDay.title: Where to go
items: On the first morning, go to registration before anything else. It opens at 7:45 am (place TBC).
Someone from the Secretariat will show you to your committee room.

phrasesIntro: Not sure what to say? Read these out as they're written, with your own country's name.

phrases.text: The delegate of India would like to be added to the speakers list.

phrases.when: To ask for a moderated caucus
phrases.text: Motion for a moderated caucus on [topic], total time 10 minutes, speaking time 1 minute.
The delegate yields the floor back to the chair.

phrases.when: To ask another delegate a question
phrases.text: Point of information to the delegate of France.

glossary.definition: What you say at roll call. "Present and voting" means you won't abstain when the committee votes on a draft resolution.
The card with your country's name on it. You raise it to speak, to answer roll call and to vote.
Short for General Speakers List: the list of countries waiting to give a speech.
A short debate on one part of the topic, where the chair picks each speaker.
Free time to leave your seat, talk to other delegates and write together.
Giving away the rest of your speaking time: to the chair, to another delegate or to questions.
Used when you think the rules weren't followed correctly.
A question to a delegate about the speech they just gave.
Used when something stops you taking part, for example if you can't hear the speaker or the room is too cold.
A group of countries that agree with each other and work together.
A first draft of a bloc's ideas, with no set format.
A working paper written in the proper format and supported by enough countries to be debated and voted on.
A line at the start of a resolution that explains the problem and what has already been done. Each one starts with a word like "Recognising" or "Noting".
A numbered line that says what the committee will do. Each one starts with a verb like "Encourages" or "Calls upon".
